name: Cabergoline

lead: Cabergoline is an ergot-derived dopamine D2 agonist taken by mouth. Its labelled use is for high prolactin, including from pituitary adenomas. In muscle and TRT communities it is discussed as a way to manage prolactin during hormone therapy, so the regimen runs smoothly and supports muscle and libido goals.

The chain: it stimulates D2 receptors on prolactin-producing pituitary cells, mimicking dopamine and lowering prolactin; in prolactinomas it also shrinks tumours. Its half-life is long, reported around 63 to 115 hours. Published trials are in prolactinomas and other pituitary conditions, not in healthy people seeking appearance changes.

paras: It is taken by mouth under a prescriber's direction, usually alongside blood work that tracks prolactin. People using it in hormone regimens treat it as a supporting drug rather than a main one.

Common effects are nausea, headache, dizziness and constipation. Ergot-derived dopamine agonists have been linked to cardiac valve regurgitation, mainly at high Parkinson's-disease doses, and the label advises cardiovascular evaluation including echocardiography. Rare pulmonary and other fibrotic complications are reported. It is prescription-only.

social.title: Cabergoline: A Drug May Reduce The Risk of Breast Cancer

angle.text: Cabergoline lowers prolactin and is discussed as an add-on to testosterone or other hormone regimens to manage prolactin side effects. The looks link is indirect: a smoother regimen is meant to support muscle and libido goals. Trials have studied it in prolactinomas.

lead: Cabergoline is an ergoline-derived dopamine D2 receptor agonist taken by mouth, sold under brand names such as Dostinex and Cabaser [1][2]. It lowers the pituitary hormone prolactin, and the US drug label lists its indication as hyperprolactinemic disorders, either idiopathic or due to pituitary adenomas [3]. It is on the World Health Organization's essential medicines list, according to Wikipedia [2].

Its link to appearance runs through hormones. Clinical sources describe high prolactin as a cause of low libido, erectile problems, reduced gonadal function and, in men, sometimes breast enlargement (gynecomastia) [4][5][6]. People on testosterone replacement or anabolic regimens sometimes discuss cabergoline when blood tests show raised prolactin, with the stated aim of protecting libido, mood and a lean, male-looking chest and physique [7][8][9]. These are community claims; the medical literature studies cabergoline in people with prolactin disorders and other disease states, not in healthy people seeking an appearance outcome.

For prolactinomas, a 2017 JAMA review states that initial therapy is generally a dopamine agonist [10], and a 2025 Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology review describes cabergoline as typically the primary therapy, normalising prolactin, shrinking the adenoma by at least 30 percent and restoring gonadal function in most patients after at least six months of treatment [7]. A 1994 double-blind trial of 459 women with hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea compared cabergoline with bromocriptine [11]. Wikipedia reports that the drug was synthesised by Farmitalia-Carlo Erba in Milan, patented in 1980, marketed in the Netherlands in 1992 and approved by the FDA in December 1996 [2].

Safety debates centre on cardiac valve disease. Two 2007 studies in Parkinson's disease patients found associations between pergolide and cabergoline and valve regurgitation [12][13], and pergolide was withdrawn from the US market that year [14]. Cabergoline has also been studied in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, acromegaly and Cushing's disease [15][16][17].

paras: Cabergoline is a long-acting, orally taken ergot-derived dopamine agonist. Wikipedia lists its approved or established uses as suppression of lactation, hyperprolactinemia, adjunct therapy for prolactinomas, early and advanced Parkinson's disease (in some countries), and as an adjunct in acromegaly, noting that it is often chosen over the older drug bromocriptine because of higher D2 affinity, fewer side effects and simpler dosing [2]. Veterinary versions are used for false pregnancy in dogs [2].

In the US it is a prescription-only drug [2][3]. The brand names Dostinex (Pfizer/Pharmacia) and Cabaser are the best known; generic tablets became available in late 2005 after patent expiry in the United States [2].

Its main use is hyperprolactinemia and prolactinoma [3][10]. It is also used for lactation suppression in some countries, and in some countries for Parkinson's disease, although its use there has declined because of valvulopathy concerns [2][18]. Randomised trials have examined it for preventing lactation after pregnancy loss and for postpartum lactation inhibition [19]. Wikipedia lists off-label uses including counteracting SSRI-related sexual side effects, possibly shortening the male refractory period, reducing ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome incidence in IVF (not its severity), and restless legs syndrome [2]. In acromegaly, where hyperprolactinemia occurs in a minority of cases, it has been used on its own or with other drugs [2][20].

Muscle and TRT-focused communities discuss dopamine agonists such as cabergoline for managing prolactin during hormone therapy [8][9]. Users describe seeking a prescription after blood work shows a high prolactin number, and some describe being on it for months alongside testosterone therapy [21]. The appearance rationale offered is indirect: prolactin is linked in clinical sources with reduced libido and gonadal suppression, and men on anabolic regimens often worry about gynecomastia, so keeping prolactin in range is framed as protecting a lean male chest and drive for training [4][6]. Wikipedia's gynecomastia article notes that high prolactin has been linked to breast enlargement but is uncommon in men presenting with it, so prolactin is usually measured but rarely the explanation [6]. No trial data exist for this use in healthy people.

Cabergoline was developed at Farmitalia-Carlo Erba in Milan, with a patent application filed in 1980. It first appeared in the literature in a 1991 Society for Neuroscience abstract and was marketed as Dostinex in the Netherlands in 1992; Farmitalia was acquired by Pharmacia in 1993 and Pharmacia by Pfizer in 2003 [2]. The FDA approved it on December 23, 1996 [2]. It is a longer-acting alternative to bromocriptine, an older ergot dopamine agonist; the 1994 comparison trial helped establish it as better tolerated in hyperprolactinemic women [11].

In 2007, two NEJM studies tied dopamine agonists used in Parkinson's disease to cardiac valve regurgitation [12][13]. The FDA announced the voluntary withdrawal of pergolide from the US market in March 2007 citing possible heart valve damage [14]. Cabergoline remained available because its US approval is for hyperprolactinemia, a setting with lower doses, but its use in Parkinson's disease declined [2][18].

sections.h: Prolactin in the physique and TRT context
paras: Prolactin is a pituitary hormone released under tonic inhibition by dopamine. Clinical reviews describe high prolactin as a common cause of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and cabergoline restores gonadal function in prolactin-secreting tumours [7][22]. Wikipedia lists drugs as the most common non-tumour cause of raised prolactin, including antipsychotics, metoclopramide and some antidepressants, with physiological causes including stress and exercise [5]. Upper normal prolactin is roughly 15 to 25 ng/mL in both sexes, and macroprolactin, an inactive complex, can falsely raise lab results [5].

Forum threads on T Nation describe users on testosterone therapy or anabolic cycles who found raised prolactin on blood tests and discussed cabergoline with their doctors, with some saying their prolactin rose after starting TRT [8][9]. In one 2020 thread a poster who had previously been treated for a prolactinoma said prolactin roughly doubled on TRT and that adjusting cabergoline helped, while another said TRT can raise prolactin through higher estrogen [9]. Other posters recommend vitamin B6 (P5P) or mucuna pruriens as alternatives [23]. A poster in another thread called cabergoline dangerous because of heart-valve effects [24]; the valve concern is documented in the label and in Parkinson's disease studies, where doses were higher than those used for hyperprolactinemia [3][12][13].

In the 1994 comparison trial, cabergoline was tested against bromocriptine in 459 women with hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea in a double-blind design [11]. A 2023 review reports that dopamine agonists, mainly cabergoline, induce disease control and restore fertility in both sexes and permanently cure about one-third of patients, allowing treatment to stop [22]. Wikipedia reports that dopamine agonists normalise prolactin and shrink tumours in about 80 percent of prolactinoma patients, and that prolactin often rises again if treatment stops [4]. Surgery is considered when drugs fail or are not tolerated [7][4].

Registered trials have explored rapid dose escalation in macroprolactinomas [25], higher-dose treatment in microprolactinomas [26], and dopamine agonists for non-functioning pituitary adenomas [27]. A 2023 JAMA review of pituitary adenomas reports that about 53 percent are prolactinomas [28].

The US label reports that most adverse events in more than 900 hyperprolactinemic patients were mild or moderate, with a dose-related effect seen only for nausea [3]. Wikipedia lists nausea, vertigo, constipation and somnolence among commonly reported effects, with rare pleural, pulmonary and pericardial fibrosis (under 2 percent in Parkinson's studies) [2]. In a roughly 200-patient Parkinson's monotherapy study 76 percent reported at least one side effect, at doses much higher than those used for hyperprolactinemia [2].

The label's warnings advise cardiovascular evaluation, including an echocardiogram, to look for valvular disease before treatment, and say patients with detected valvular disease should not be treated [3]. A UK population-based cohort of 11,417 patients and an echocardiographic study of 155 patients with Parkinson's disease both reported increased valve regurgitation with ergot-derived agonists [12][13]. Wikipedia reports that low doses used for hyperprolactinemia were not linked to clinically significant valve disease [2]. Contraindications include ergot hypersensitivity and severe liver impairment, and dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide can counteract its effects [2].

Cabergoline is a potent D2 agonist that also binds D3, D4 and several serotonin receptors, including 5-HT2B, which has been linked to valvulopathy [2][29]. Wikipedia reports that the same 5-HT2B agonism is thought to underlie valve damage with pergolide, ergotamine and fenfluramine [14]. Oral bioavailability is reported at 50 to 80 percent, with hepatic metabolism and mostly faecal excretion; elimination half-life is about 63 to 69 hours in Parkinson's patients and 79 to 115 hours in pituitary tumour patients [2]. The long half-life is why it is dosed far less often than bromocriptine [2][11].

The US label places cabergoline in Category B, with animal studies showing maternal toxicity but no teratogenic effects at the doses tested [3]. Wikipedia notes that data are limited and that bromocriptine is often preferred in pregnancy because of more safety data [2].

Human trials are in disease populations: hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea [11], Parkinson's disease [12][13], prolactinoma dosing [25][26], non-functioning pituitary adenomas [27], metastatic breast cancer [30], acromegaly [17][20], ovarian hyperstimulation in polycystic ovary syndrome [15], lactation inhibition [19] and Cushing's disease [16][31]. A 2006 pharmacological study used cabergoline to probe dopamine function in human cognition [32]. No studies found for appearance or physique outcomes in healthy people. A 2025 review and a 2023 clinical endocrinology review describe cabergoline as primary therapy for prolactinoma [7][22].

Cabergoline is prescription-only in the US and in Australia (Schedule 4) [2]. Discussion in TRT and bodybuilding forums often includes users describing getting a prescription through a clinic or doctor after lab work [8][9]; these are individual reports and the regulatory indication remains hyperprolactinemic disorders [3]. Clinicians in the reviews cited stress diagnosis, imaging and specialist follow-up when prolactin is raised [22][5].

lore.intro: On T Nation, cabergoline appears in TRT and cycle threads as a prolactin-lowering option [8][9][24].

claims.claim: Cabergoline is needed to control prolactin on TRT or certain anabolics.
Cabergoline carries a serious heart-valve risk.
Vitamin B6 (P5P) or mucuna can replace cabergoline for lowering prolactin.
High prolactin on TRT can sap libido and needs to be treated.
Cabergoline keeps the chest lean by preventing gynecomastia.
Cabergoline at high-dose Parkinson's levels and at low hyperprolactinemia levels carry the same valve risk.
